title: Biosphere — Life on the Earth
tagline: The thin zone where land, water and air meet, its ecosystems, biomes, food chains and the human pressure on them.

overview.intro: The biosphere is the portion of the Earth where life exists, and it is remarkably thin: it reaches only a few kilometres up, a few kilometres down into rock, and covers the whole of the hydrosphere. Life is possible there because the right temperature range, liquid water, an atmosphere containing oxygen and carbon dioxide, and a supply of nutrients all coincide. This unit covers the conditions required for life, the ecosystems and biomes that organise living communities, the flow of energy through food chains and food webs, and the human activities that are currently disturbing the balance.

facts.label: Extent
facts.value: The biosphere spans the lower atmosphere, the whole hydrosphere and the upper part of the crust, and it is the only zone where all three spheres meet.

facts.label: Ecosystem
facts.value: A community of organisms together with the physical environment with which they interact, through which energy flows and nutrients cycle.

facts.label: Energy loss
facts.value: Roughly 90 per cent of energy is lost at each transfer between trophic levels, mainly as heat, which limits chain length.

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: Habitat loss, pollution, over-exploitation and invasive species are the principal human threats to the biosphere.

learningOutcomes: State the conditions required for life on Earth.
Define ecosystem and distinguish its biotic and abiotic components.
Explain energy flow through food chains and the ecological pyramid.
Assess the human pressures on the biosphere.

learn.title: Conditions for life and the structure of an ecosystem

blocks.text: Life on Earth depends on a narrow band of conditions. Liquid water must be available, since every biochemical reaction takes place in it, and water is liquid only between 0 and 100 degrees Celsius at ordinary pressure. The temperature range of the surface must stay moderate, which is where the atmosphere and the ocean’s heat capacity matter. An atmosphere must supply oxygen for respiration and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, and soil or water must supply the mineral nutrients that plants need. Solar radiation drives the whole system by providing the energy for photosynthesis.

An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with their physical environment as a single functional unit. Its biotic components are the producers, which are green plants that fix solar energy; the consumers, which are animals that feed on plants or on each other; and the decomposers, which break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil and water. Its abiotic components are the non-living factors such as light, temperature, moisture, soil, pH and minerals, which limit what can live where.

learn.title: Food chains, food webs and ecological pyramids

blocks.text: Energy passes from the sun to producers and then along a food chain of consumers, but the transfer is inefficient. At each step much of the energy is used for respiration and lost as heat, so only about a tenth passes to the next level. This is why food chains rarely exceed four or five links, and why there are far fewer top predators than herbivores. A food web recognises that most organisms eat more than one thing, so chains interlock into a network whose stability depends on the number of alternative paths.

Ecological pyramids represent the relationship graphically. The pyramid of numbers shows how many organisms exist at each level, and it may be inverted, as when one large tree supports many insects. The pyramid of biomass shows the dry weight of living matter at each level, which is normally upright for land ecosystems. The pyramid of energy is always upright, because energy decreases at each transfer, and it is the most reliable of the three.

blocks.text: A biome is a large community of plants and animals occupying a major habitat, defined chiefly by climate and especially by the balance of temperature and rainfall. Tropical rainforest grows where rainfall is high and temperature is uniform through the year, supporting the greatest diversity of species. Tropical savanna has a distinct dry season and grassland with scattered trees, and its animals migrate with the rains. Deserts receive under 250 millimetres of rain a year, so life is sparse and adapted to conserve water. Temperate grassland, or steppe, has hot summers, cold winters and moderate rainfall, and its deep soils are among the most productive farmland on Earth.

blocks.text: Human activity now alters the biosphere faster than many ecosystems can adapt. Deforestation removes habitat and the carbon storage in trees, while also changing local rainfall through reduced transpiration. Pollution of air, water and soil poisons organisms and can accumulate through food chains. Over-exploitation of fish stocks and wildlife reduces populations below the level at which they can recover. Finally, the alteration of the atmosphere through greenhouse emissions is changing temperature and precipitation patterns worldwide, shifting the boundaries of biomes faster than species can migrate.

items: Protect habitat through reserves and corridors that join fragmented patches.
Reduce emissions and increase carbon storage in forests and soils.
Set harvest limits for fisheries and wildlife at sustainable levels.
Treat waste before discharge and recycle nutrients rather than losing them.
Restore degraded land rather than opening new land for cultivation.

keyPoints: The biosphere is the thin zone where atmosphere, hydrosphere and crust meet and life exists.
Liquid water, a moderate temperature range, an atmosphere with oxygen and carbon dioxide, and nutrients are the conditions for life.
An ecosystem has biotic components of producers, consumers and decomposers and abiotic factors that limit them.
Energy flows one way through a chain and is eventually lost as heat; nutrients cycle.
About 10 per cent of energy passes between trophic levels, which limits chain length.
A pyramid of energy can never be inverted; pyramids of numbers and biomass sometimes can.
Biomes are defined chiefly by temperature and rainfall.
Deserts receive under 250 mm of rain a year and support sparse, water-conserving life.
Deforestation, pollution, over-exploitation and greenhouse emissions are the main human pressures.
Ecosystem services such as water filtration and flood buffering are lost when habitats are removed.
examFocus: Energy-flow questions must quote the percentage lost at each transfer and explain why chains stay short.
Biome answers should link the vegetation to the controlling climate figures rather than listing plants.
Human-pressure questions gain marks by pairing each pressure with the consequence, not the cause alone.

questions.prompt: In an ecosystem the organisms that convert solar energy into organic matter are the:
questions.explanation: Green plants and algae photosynthesise, fixing solar energy into the organic matter on which every other level depends.

questions.prompt: Approximately what proportion of energy passes from one trophic level to the next?
questions.explanation: Around a tenth is transferred and the rest is used in respiration and lost as heat, which is why chains are short.

questions.prompt: Which ecological pyramid can never be inverted?
questions.explanation: Energy is lost at every transfer, so the energy available always decreases upward, whatever happens to counts or biomass.

questions.prompt: A biome with under 250 mm of rainfall, extreme diurnal temperature range and vegetation adapted to conserve water is:
questions.explanation: Desert life is sparse and adapted through deep roots, spines and reduced leaf surface because water is the limiting factor.

questions.prompt: The thin zone of the Earth in which life exists, where the three spheres meet, is called the __________ .
questions.explanation: It extends only a few kilometres up into the atmosphere and down into the crust, and includes the whole hydrosphere.

questions.prompt: The build-up of a substance such as a pesticide in an organism, concentrating it higher up a food chain, is called bio __________ .
questions.explanation: Because the substance is not excreted, each level of the chain carries a higher concentration than the one below.

questions.prompt: State four conditions necessary for life on Earth.
questions.answer: Four conditions are: liquid water, since biochemical reactions occur in solution; a moderate range of surface temperature, kept narrow by the atmosphere and ocean; an atmosphere supplying oxygen for respiration and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis; and soil or water supplying mineral nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus. Solar radiation as the energy source is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each condition needs a line explaining why it is necessary, since naming alone earns only partial credit.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a food chain and a food web.
questions.answer: A food chain is a single linear sequence showing how energy passes from one organism to the next, such as grass to grasshopper to frog to snake to hawk, with each link at one trophic level. A food web is a network of such chains linked together, because most organisms feed on more than one kind of food and are eaten by more than one predator. A food web is the more realistic representation, and its greater number of alternative paths makes an ecosystem more stable, since the loss of one species does not necessarily break the flow of energy.
questions.explanation: The comparison must cover structure and the consequence of that structure for stability.

questions.prompt: Explain the flow of energy in an ecosystem and the pyramids used to represent it.
questions.answer: Energy enters an ecosystem as solar radiation, and green producers capture roughly one per cent of it through photosynthesis, converting it into organic matter. Primary consumers eat the producers and obtain about a tenth of the energy stored in them; the rest is used in respiration or lost as heat. The same loss occurs at each subsequent level, so only about a tenth passes upward each time, which is why food chains rarely exceed four or five links and why top predators are always rare. The relationship is shown by three pyramids. The pyramid of numbers counts organisms at each level and can be inverted when one large producer supports many small consumers. The pyramid of biomass measures dry weight and is normally upright on land but may be inverted in water where producers turn over very rapidly. The pyramid of energy is always upright, because energy must decrease at every transfer, and it is therefore the most reliable of the three.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the percentage of transfer, the reason chains are short, and all three pyramids with their possibility of inversion.

questions.prompt: A valley is cleared of forest for farming, a factory upstream discharges effluent into the river, and the fish population then collapses. Analyse the case using ecosystem components, energy flow and a human pressure, and recommend two remedies.
questions.answer: The clearance removes the producer level of the terrestrial ecosystem, so the energy input that supported insects, birds and soil organisms is cut, and the exposed soil loses nutrients through erosion rather than having them recycled by decomposers. The effluent changes the abiotic conditions of the river, since dissolved oxygen falls as bacteria consume the waste, and the water chemistry no longer suits the fish, which are the secondary consumers of that system. The collapse of fish then removes the prey of birds and other predators, so a disturbance at one level propagates through the food web, which shows that energy flow and species are linked rather than independent. Two remedies follow directly: treat the effluent before discharge so that dissolved oxygen and nutrient levels remain within the range aquatic life tolerates, and reforest the cleared slopes with a buffer strip of native vegetation along the river, which holds soil, filters runoff and restores the producer base. A third useful step would be setting a harvest limit while the population recovers, since a stock below its recovery level cannot be fished sustainably.
questions.explanation: Marks require mapping each act onto a component of the ecosystem, tracing the effect through the food web, and giving remedies that address the cause rather than the symptom.
